claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by formation of a non-protective, compositionally heterogeneous oxide scale.
Oxide scale formation preferentially occurs along grain boundaries.
Additive manufacturing produces grain-boundary microsegregation of Al, Ti, and Cr in the starting alloy.
The as-built alloy has a homogeneous FCC matrix overall.
Local enrichment or depletion of Al, Ti, and Cr produces grain-boundary oxide layers.
Small grain-boundary compositional inhomogeneities promote rapid localized oxidation.
Oxidizing exposure produces a multilayered or porous scale containing mixed Al2O3 and Cr2O3.
The oxide scale is poorly adherent and undergoes continuous spallation.
A reducing atmosphere thins or destabilizes the nascent oxide scale.
Scale thinning or instability in reducing gas exposes the substrate to further reaction and grain-boundary microcracking.
The proposed surface degradation mechanism does not substantially alter the bulk FCC matrix.
Retention of the bulk FCC matrix preserves the alloy's overall strength and fatigue properties during exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will cause progressive grain-boundary oxidation, spallation, and a non-uniform multilayered scale.
Reducing exposure will produce a thinner, less-adherent or partially reduced scale accompanied by grain-boundary microcracking.
The as-manufactured baseline has minimal oxide content and only subtle grain-boundary microsegregation.
The proposed mechanism dominates above approximately 700 °C when gas-reaction kinetics outpace bulk homogenization.
Processing that eliminates microsegregation will shift or reduce the degradation behavior.
Homogenization heat treatment should reduce grain-boundary elemental fluctuations and consequently reduce oxide-scale heterogeneity and degradation.
